title: Firewall Investigation

theory.concept: Firewall logs record allow and deny decisions per session, plus the rule that made the decision. Analysts use them for three things: proving whether an attempted connection actually succeeded, finding permissive legacy rules nobody owns, and confirming or dismissing volume-based alerts. A DENY is evidence the control worked; an ALLOW on a path that should not exist is a finding in itself.
theory.why: Blocking is the fastest containment lever a SOC has, but blocking the wrong flow can stop payroll or replication. You must be certain which rule and which traffic you are touching.
look: Rules with no owner, no ticket and a creation date years old
ALLOW decisions on inbound management protocols (445, 3389, 22) from the internet
Large sustained transfers to external addresses outside backup windows
Deny bursts across sequential ports (scanning) versus deny bursts on one port (misconfigured client)
fp: Backup replication, SaaS sync and video conferencing generate enormous, entirely legitimate volumes
A newly deployed application will trip volume rules until the baseline updates
tips: Always check the change calendar and the destination's business relationship before calling a transfer exfiltration.
Record the rule name in your report - remediation is owned by the network team and they need the rule ID.

case.alert: Large outbound data transfer to external address outside business hours
case.brief: A volume-threshold rule fired on the finance file server: 412 GB outbound to an external address overnight. The overnight analyst flagged it as possible exfiltration. Validate or dismiss that assessment, and review the perimeter ruleset while you are in there.

The genuinely alarming findings in this case are not in the alert you were given - they are in the ruleset extract.
review: The 412 GB transfer is contracted DR replication: same destination, same rule, same 02:00 window, comparable volume on 22 and 15 February, valid certificate for a domain in the contract register. It closes as a False Positive - but the case is not a waste of time, because the ruleset review is where the value is. FW-LEGACY-11 is an ownerless 2021 'temporary' rule allowing SMB from the entire internet to a domain controller, and it is how the svc_backup compromise reached DC-01. FW-MGMT-03 allowed the SSH intrusion, and the permissive FW-EGRESS-ANY is why C2 traffic leaves unchallenged. Findings from a False Positive investigation still go in the report.

title: Endpoint Investigation

theory.concept: An EDR agent records process creation, file writes, registry changes, module loads and network connections, linked into a process tree. Endpoint investigation means reconstructing that tree: what ran, what started it, what it wrote to disk, and what it contacted. The parent chain is usually the whole story.
theory.why: The endpoint is where user, file, process and network evidence intersect. It is the only place you can see initial access and execution in the same view.
look: Execution from user-writable paths: %TEMP%, %APPDATA%, C:\Users\Public, %PROGRAMDATA%
Office applications or browsers as parents of script interpreters or cmd.exe
Binaries with mismatched or missing digital signatures, or names imitating system files (svch0st.exe, rundll32 copies)
File writes immediately followed by execution of the same file
Unsigned processes making outbound TLS connections to raw IPs
fp: Installers legitimately drop and execute from %TEMP%
Developer tooling spawns interpreters constantly - check the user and the host role
tips: Note the exact file path and hash; they become IOCs for the estate-wide sweep.
Attackers name payloads after real Windows components. Verify the path, not the name.

title: Phishing Investigation

theory.concept: Email investigation works from the headers outward. The Return-Path and the authentication results (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) establish whether the message really came from the domain it claims. The Received chain shows the actual path. The body and its links show intent. Display names are free text and prove nothing.
theory.why: Phishing remains the most common initial access vector. Scoping a campaign quickly - who received it, who clicked, who submitted credentials - decides whether it stays one incident or becomes twelve.
look: Look-alike domains: character substitution, extra hyphens, plausible new TLDs
SPF/DKIM/DMARC failures, especially DMARC fail with a mismatched Return-Path
Received hops through unrelated infrastructure
Attachment types that execute: .lnk, .iso, .img, .html, macro-enabled Office documents, password-protected archives that bypass scanning
Urgency, authority and secrecy in the body text
fp: Legitimate bulk mail and marketing platforms routinely fail DKIM alignment when misconfigured
Forwarded internal mail breaks SPF by design - check whether the forwarding host is your own
tips: Scope by sender domain, subject and attachment hash, then by who actually clicked.
Password-protected archives with the password in the email body exist to defeat content scanning.

The payload is a .lnk inside a password-protected ZIP, a combination chosen specifically to defeat gateway scanning. Two users executed it: k.rahman (already known) and m.chen in Finance - which explains how the intrusion reached the finance file server. j.almeida reported it correctly and that behaviour should be reinforced publicly.

title: Malware Indicators

theory.concept: Static triage examines a sample without running it: hashes for identification, imports for capability, strings for infrastructure and behaviour, packing and entropy for evasion, compile timestamp and certificate for provenance. Dynamic triage runs it in a sandbox and records what it actually does. A Tier-1 analyst is not expected to reverse engineer, but is expected to read a triage report and pull indicators out of it.
theory.why: The report converts one infected machine into detection content for the whole estate.
look: Imports that reveal capability: CreateRemoteThread and VirtualAllocEx for injection, CryptEncrypt for ransomware, InternetOpenUrl for download
High entropy sections and a packer such as UPX
Strings containing URLs, IPs, mutex names, user-agents and file paths
Compile timestamp close to first-seen date (freshly built) or absurdly old (faked)
Mutex creation - a unique mutex is an excellent, very cheap detection
fp: Packers are used by plenty of commercial software
Sandbox reports flag benign behaviour like reading the registry; judge the combination, not one line
tips: Turn every extracted artefact into a hunt query: hash, mutex, user-agent, domain, file path.
A hardcoded user-agent string is often the most durable indicator in the whole sample.

review: STORMPETREL is a loader: it establishes persistence via an HKCU Run value named WinUpdateSvc, ensures a single instance with the mutex Global\NWSYNC_9F21, beacons POST /gate.php to cdn-sync-delivery[.]net every 600 seconds with 12 seconds of jitter, injects into explorer.exe to survive process termination, and profiles the host including which AV is installed. The injection triple (VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, CreateRemoteThread) confirms capability that static naming alone would not. Crucially it does not encrypt anything - this is an access tool, meaning a human operator is expected to follow. The campaign-specific mutex and the NorthSync/2.1 user-agent are the highest-value detections because they survive recompilation; the SHA256 will not.
next: You now hold a full indicator set. The next task is to pivot on those indicators across every data source you have touched so far, and find hosts nobody has flagged yet.

title: IOC Investigation

theory.concept: An indicator of compromise is any observable that ties an environment to known malicious activity: hashes, IPs, domains, URLs, registry values, mutexes, file paths, user-agents, certificate fingerprints. Pivoting is the discipline of taking one confirmed indicator, searching every data source for it, and using each new hit to generate the next search.
theory.why: Pivoting is how scoping happens. Without it you contain the machines you already knew about and leave the rest infected.
look: The same indicator appearing in a data source nobody has checked yet
Hosts matching a behavioural indicator (mutex, Run key, user-agent) even where the file hash differs
Time gaps: a host that beaconed once a week ago and stopped is still compromised
Indicators appearing on assets outside the originally scoped department
fp: Shared infrastructure - a CDN IP may host both malicious and legitimate content, so IP-only matching over-scopes
Security tooling and researchers inside your estate may legitimately touch malicious domains
tips: Record indicator confidence: a campaign-specific mutex is high confidence, a shared hosting IP is low.
Every pivot needs a written source and timestamp; your scoping list becomes the containment list.

Three of the new hits have innocent explanations: a SOC-owned lab machine, a user who clicked but did not execute, and an unrelated product that happens to share a name.
review: Confirmed scope is three hosts. SRV-FILE02 is the important discovery: the file hash missed it because the operator deployed a rebuilt binary (nwsync.exe in C:\ProgramData, different SHA256), but the campaign-specific mutex and the NorthSync user-agent matched - exactly the durability argument from the triage report. SOC-ANALYST-VM01 matched because the SOC detonated the sample there; excluding your own tooling from scope is a routine discipline. WKS-2019 matched a substring against an unrelated analytics SaaS, the classic over-broad indicator problem. WKS-2077 resolved the domain once from chrome.exe with no execution - exposed, worth monitoring, not compromised.
next: You have three compromised hosts and a coherent indicator set. Before Tier 2 builds the response plan, the threat intelligence function wants your assessment of who is behind this and what they normally do next.

title: Threat Intelligence

theory.concept: Threat intelligence has three layers. Tactical intelligence is indicators - hashes, domains, IPs - useful immediately and short-lived. Operational intelligence is tradecraft: the tools, techniques and sequencing a group uses. Strategic intelligence is targeting and motive. Attribution is a confidence judgement, never a certainty, and is expressed in language that reflects that.
theory.why: Knowing what an actor normally does next turns reactive containment into anticipation. If the group historically deploys ransomware on day four, day three is not the time for a leisurely change-approval process.
look: Overlap of infrastructure, tooling and tradecraft across incidents, not a single shared IP
Targeting patterns: sector, geography, company size
Typical dwell time and the ordering of stages
Known handoff behaviour - initial access brokers selling to ransomware affiliates
fp: Shared hosting, commodity malware and public tooling are used by many unrelated actors
Actor names differ between vendors; the same group may carry four names
tips: State confidence explicitly: low, moderate, high - and say what would change your mind.
Use intelligence to prioritise, never to skip evidence you have not actually collected.

case.alert: Attribution and predictive assessment requested by Incident Manager
case.brief: Assess which known actor this activity most closely matches, with a confidence level, and state what the SOC should expect next. Your assessment drives whether this incident goes to the crisis process.

evidence.name: Observed Tradecraft (this incident)
rows: Initial access: spearphishing, password-protected ZIP containing .lnk, look-alike partner domain
Execution: PowerShell downloader -> UPX-packed loader in %TEMP%
Persistence: HKCU Run value; Linux cron entry
C2: HTTPS POST /gate.php, 600s +/- 12s jitter, user-agent NorthSync/2.1, self-signed certificate
Credential access: NTLM brute force against a service account from external infrastructure
Targets touched: logistics workstations, production Linux API server, finance file server

evidence.name: CTI Actor Profiles
rows: TA-4411 (aka STORMPETREL): financially motivated, targets logistics and freight in South and Central Asia. TTPs: partner-impersonation phishing with .lnk in encrypted archives, custom UPX loader, /gate.php C2 with branded user-agents, NTLM brute force on service accounts. Typical dwell 4-7 days, then data theft followed by extortion. 3 prior incidents share the NorthSync user-agent.

TA-2290 (aka GLASSHOUR): espionage, targets government and defence in Europe. TTPs: zero-day exploitation of edge devices, in-memory implants only, no persistence on disk, DNS-over-HTTPS C2. No phishing observed.
TA-8801 (aka REDSILT): hacktivist, targets media. TTPs: web defacement, credential stuffing from public dumps, no custom malware.
Commodity infostealer crews: opportunistic, broad phishing, off-the-shelf loaders, no follow-on human operator.

evidence.name: Incident-Specific Signals
rows: Operator activity is human-driven and interactive (manual sudo commands, directory enumeration), not fully automated
Second-stage binary rebuilt with a different hash but identical mutex - indicates active development during the intrusion
DNS tunnelling from the finance file server began 2 hours after that host was reached
No encryption or destructive activity observed as of 13:00 on day 1

questions.label: Which actor profile best matches the observed tradecraft?
questions.hint: Compare initial access, C2 style and targeting sector against each profile.

questions.label: Which single technical artefact links this incident to prior incidents by that actor?
questions.hint: One profile explicitly names an artefact shared with three prior incidents.

questions.label: What is the actor's assessed motivation?
questions.hint: Read the first line of the matching profile.

questions.label: Based on the profile, what should the SOC expect next?
questions.hint: The profile states the typical sequence after dwell time.

questions.label: Why can TA-2290 be ruled out?
questions.hint: Compare the persistence and access methods - two profiles are almost opposites.

questions.label: What confidence level is appropriate for this attribution?
questions.hint: Multiple independent overlaps - tooling, user-agent, sector, tradecraft - but attribution is never 'confirmed'.

questions.label: Given the typical dwell time, how urgent is containment?
questions.hint: Compare the profile's 4-7 day dwell with the fact that you are on day 1 and exfiltration has already started.

recommend.text: Escalate to Incident Manager as a major incident with high-confidence TA-4411 attribution, accelerate containment ahead of the expected exfiltration/extortion stage, and brief legal and executive stakeholders.

hints: Attribution is comparison. Line up initial access, persistence style, C2 pattern and target sector against each profile and discard the ones that contradict what you observed.
Intelligence is only useful if it changes a decision. Ask what the profile says happens after the dwell period, then ask what day of the intrusion you are on.
review: TA-4411 (STORMPETREL) matches on every axis: partner-impersonation phishing with an encrypted archive and .lnk, UPX-packed loader, /gate.php C2 with a branded user-agent, NTLM brute force against a service account, and logistics sector targeting in the right region. The NorthSync/2.1 user-agent appearing in three prior incidents is the strongest single link. GLASSHOUR is excluded because it uses no phishing and leaves nothing on disk; REDSILT has no custom malware at all; commodity crews do not feature a human operator typing sudo commands. High confidence is appropriate - multiple independent overlaps - but the assessment should still name what would change it. The decision that matters is escalation: this actor steals and extorts after four to seven days, DNS tunnelling from the finance server is already running, and you are on day one.
next: The incident is now formally escalated. Tier 2 wants the execution layer pulled apart: PowerShell script block logs from WKS-2041 have been recovered, including the decoded command the loader used.

title: PowerShell Investigation

theory.concept: PowerShell is the attacker's preferred execution layer on Windows because it is present, signed and powerful. Defenders get three logging channels: module logging (4103), script block logging (4104, which records the actual code after de-obfuscation), and transcription. Event 4104 is the single most valuable Windows log for execution analysis.
theory.why: Encoded commands are unreadable in 4688 command lines but appear in plain text in 4104. Knowing to look there is the difference between 'something ran' and 'here is exactly what it did'.
look: -EncodedCommand / -enc with a base64 blob, -w hidden, -nop, -ExecutionPolicy Bypass
Download cradles: Invoke-WebRequest, iwr, DownloadString, Net.WebClient, Invoke-RestMethod
In-memory execution: IEX, Invoke-Expression, [Reflection.Assembly]::Load, FromBase64String
Concatenation and string reversal used to break signatures
AMSI bypass attempts and event log clearing
fp: Administrators and deployment tooling use Bypass and encoded commands legitimately - check the parent process and the user
Monitoring scripts issue web requests constantly
tips: Base64 in PowerShell is UTF-16LE; every second byte is a null, which is why decoded text can look spaced out.
4104 captures code even when it never touches disk, which is precisely the point of fileless attacks.

case.alert: Script block logging captured obfuscated PowerShell execution
case.brief: Analyse the recovered script block logs. Determine what the script actually did, what it disabled, and whether anything beyond the known loader was executed.

questions.label: What security control does the first script block attempt to disable?
questions.hint: Read the concatenated type name in block 1 - the string is split deliberately to evade detection.

questions.label: Why is the type name split with a plus sign?
questions.hint: Consider how a signature-based detection matches on literal strings.

questions.label: Which cmdlet downloads the payload?

questions.label: At 08:36 the attacker enumerated a network share. Which one?

questions.hint: Read the Get-ADUser filter.

recommend.text: Keep WKS-2041 isolated, treat the finance share enumeration as pre-exfiltration reconnaissance, hunt for the same AMSI bypass pattern estate-wide, and enforce Constrained Language Mode and script signing for non-admin users.

hints: Script block logging shows the code after de-obfuscation. Read each block as an attacker sentence: disable defences, fetch payload, persist, look around.
Four of these blocks happen well after the initial infection. They are not the loader - they are a human operator exploring the network.
review: Three blocks at 08:29 are the loader chain: an AMSI bypass (the type name split with string concatenation specifically to defeat signature matching), an Invoke-WebRequest download, then execution plus the HKCU Run persistence you already found. The later blocks are far more serious because they are interactive operator activity: enumerating spreadsheets and PDFs on the finance share at 08:36 (pre-exfiltration targeting, which explains why SRV-FILE02 was hit next), checking which event logs hold records at 08:44, fingerprinting installed EDR vendors at 09:12, and listing Domain Admins at 10:05. A Logistics user with no scripting role running any of this is conclusive.
next: The operator is enumerating and evading. To distinguish their activity from normal system behaviour, you need to be able to read process trees properly - and the next alert on the queue is going to look far worse than it is.

title: Process Analysis

theory.concept: Every Windows process has an expected parent, an expected path, an expected user and an expected frequency. Process analysis compares observed trees against that baseline. Attackers abuse legitimate signed binaries - living off the land - so the binary name alone tells you almost nothing; the relationship does.
theory.why: Both the intrusion and the IT department will spawn PowerShell, WMI and rundll32. Separating them correctly is the highest-frequency judgement a SOC analyst makes.
look: Impossible parents: winword.exe -> powershell.exe, w3wp.exe -> cmd.exe, services.exe -> unsigned binary
System binaries running from the wrong directory
lsass.exe being opened for read by anything that is not a known security product
rundll32, regsvr32, mshta, certutil used to execute or download
Correct process names running under the wrong user or integrity level
fp: Management agents, remote support tools, backup software and printer drivers produce alarming-looking trees legitimately
Vulnerability scanners with credentialed access spawn WMI and PowerShell across the estate
tips: Check the signer and the full path before reacting to a process name.
When behaviour appears identically on many hosts at the same moment, look for the management server.

case.alert: EDR: credential-access behaviour - LSASS handle opened by non-standard process
case.brief: A high-severity credential-access detection fired on an application server during an active incident. Determine whether this is the intrusion spreading or something else, and be prepared to defend your conclusion to the incident manager.

questions.label: Correct verdict for this alert
options: True Positive - credential dumping by the intruder
questions.hint: Signed tool, allowlisted path, authorised admin, MFA, matching ticket, no egress, no attacker artefacts.

recommend.text: Close as a False Positive against INC-20449, require the dump file to be secured and deleted after vendor analysis, and tune the rule to account for signed Sysinternals tooling run by admin accounts from the allowlisted path with a matching ticket.

hints: LSASS access is genuinely one of the highest-value detections in Windows - which is exactly why you must check who did it, with what binary, from where, and whether a ticket exists before escalating.
Compare this host against the attacker profile you have built over the last six cases. Ask what is missing, not only what is present.
review: This is a False Positive, and getting there under incident pressure is the skill being tested. The behaviour is real credential-access behaviour - procdump reading LSASS memory - but every contextual signal contradicts intrusion: the binary is Microsoft-signed from an allowlisted engineering path, the account is an authorised administrator who satisfied MFA four minutes earlier over internal RDP, ticket INC-20449 requested the dump 22 minutes before it happened, the dump stayed local, and none of the attacker's addresses, persistence artefacts or unsigned tooling exist on the host. The residual risk is worth documenting anyway: a 142 MB LSASS dump sitting on disk is a credential store, and it should be secured and deleted. During a live incident, the pressure to escalate everything is the thing to resist.
next: With the noise resolved, attention returns to the confirmed hosts. The operator has been quiet for two hours - which usually means persistence is already in place somewhere you have not looked. Hunt for it.
